metadata.title: Does socioeconomic sorting of teacher qualifications exacerbate mathematics achievement inequity? Panel data estimates from 20 years of TIMSS

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TIMSS microdata across six waves (1999–2019) and constructs an unbalanced grade-8 student panel linked to mathematics teachers. TIMSS employs a two-stage stratified sampling design (schools then whole classrooms), and the authors explicitly apply TIMSS mathematics teacher weights when computing teacher qualification exposure rates and qualification gaps, and TIMSS student weights when forming SES top/bottom thirds within each country-year. In the panel regression, the paper reports that student level weights were applied (Table 2 notes: “Student level weights applied”), but it does not name the exact weight variable(s) in the excerpt. Replicate weights (e.g., BRR/jackknife) are not reported; instead, the authors use robust standard errors clustered at the country level to account for clustering and the treatment at the system level.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analysis uses six TIMSS waves from 1999 to 2019, excluding 1995 due to incomplete teacher/student information. The analytic sample is restricted to education systems that participated in at least four of the six TIMSS cycles, yielding 32 education systems. Education systems with complete missing values in the target socioeconomic or teacher qualification variables in one or more cycles (Belgium, Czech Republic, Germany, Netherlands) are dropped. The initial sample size is 904,390, but duplicate students are removed after linking students to teachers in the IDB Analyzer. Missing data are handled via multivariate imputation by chained equations (mice) separately for each country-year, creating five imputed datasets per country-year (and then pooled), and remaining missing school-level controls are imputed after teacher qualification gaps are created.

main_findings.dataset_used: TIMSS 1999–2019 Grade 8 Mathematics (panel; 32 education systems with ≥4 waves)
main_findings.target_variable: Mathematics achievement (TIMSS mathematics score; inequity via SES interaction)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Panel fixed-effects OLS with country and year fixed effects; robust SE clustered by country. Key coefficients (Model 3, Table 2): SES × Teacher sorting (out-of-subject) = 44.30 (SE 24.55, t=1.81); SES × Socioeconomic school segregation = 34.81 (SE 9.78, t=3.55). Substantive average within-unit treatment effects: out-of-subject sorting ≈ 1.20 TIMSS points; socioeconomic school segregation ≈ 1.39 TIMSS points (residualized SD approach).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 1999–2019 Grade 8 Mathematics the study leveraged student SES, socioeconomic school segregation, and system-level teacher qualification gaps (especially out-of-subject mathematics teacher sorting) to model mathematics achievement inequity via an SES interaction, finding that socioeconomic teacher sorting by mathematics education significantly exacerbates achievement inequity while novice-teacher sorting shows null effects. This indicates that policies aimed at redistributing mathematics-specialized teacher qualifications toward low-SES students may reduce SES-linked math inequities, though the estimates are correlational and rely on fixed-effects assumptions rather than causal identification.

data.outcome_summary: The study uses six waves of TIMSS (1999–2019) for grade-8 mathematics, constructing an unbalanced cross-country panel across 32 education systems that participated in at least four cycles. The dependent variable is TIMSS mathematics achievement (standardized to a 500/100 scale) and the key inequity mechanism is tested by interacting student SES with system-level teacher qualification gaps (novice experience vs mathematics education specialization) and with socioeconomic school segregation. Missing data are addressed with multivariate imputation by chained equations (mice) producing five imputed datasets per country-year, and results are pooled using Rubin-style combining rules across plausible values. In fixed-effects panel regressions with country and year fixed effects and country-clustered robust SEs, out-of-subject (mathematics-education) teacher sorting significantly increases the SES–achievement association (Model 3: SES × out-of-subject sorting coefficient ≈ 44.30; SES × segregation ≈ 34.81), while novice sorting is null. The paper reports student weights applied and uses teacher weights for exposure/gap construction; however, the approach remains observational and fixed-effects estimates can still be sensitive to time-varying confounding and measurement error in teacher qualification proxies.
